explanations.answer: Tears it down with her own hands
explanations.explanation: That's the line, friend: a foolish woman "tears it down with her own hands." No storm, no wrecking crew, just her. The wise woman builds up the very same house the foolish one pulls apart. Same house, different hands.

explanations.answer: Leaves it standing empty for years
explanations.explanation: The proverb never says anything about an empty house or about years. It says the foolish woman "tears it down with her own hands." This house doesn't sit there waiting. It comes down, and she's the one who brings it down.

explanations.answer: Hands it over to her neighbor
explanations.explanation: No neighbor shows up in this proverb at all. The foolish woman keeps her hands busy, and not on a handoff. The text says she "tears it down with her own hands." Everything in the house stays between her and the house.

Yes, the proverb says it plainly. The man who walks in uprightness fears the LORD, "but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him." Two men, two directions, and the text puts the LORD right in the middle of the contrast.

The proverb says the opposite of what this card claims. The upright man is the one who fears the LORD, "but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him." So the devious man is the one who despises the LORD. Easy one to flip when you read it fast, friend.

Right. "The proud speech of a fool brings a rod to his back." His own mouth sends the bill. The same verse says "the lips of the wise protect them," so the mouth can be a shield or a problem, depending on whose it is.

The proverb doesn't give the proud fool any followers. It says his proud speech "brings a rod to his back." The only crowd that mouth gathers is a crowd of trouble. The wise get the protection, and the fool gets the rod.
Ease sounds nice, but the proverb has something else in mind. The fool's proud speech "brings a rod to his back." That's not exactly a spa day. It's the lips of the wise that protect them.

That's it. "An abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." An empty manger might look neat, but there's no harvest coming from it. Strength costs something, and the ox is where the harvest comes from.
Dust is about all you'd get from that empty manger, I'll give you that. But the proverb says "an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." The ox is the reason the field pays off.

Pasture is a good guess, since oxen and fields go together. But the proverb says what comes through the strength of the ox is "an abundant harvest." The manger is empty without oxen, and the harvest is what the ox brings in.

That's what the text says: "A mocker seeks wisdom and finds none." He goes out looking and comes back with empty hands. Meanwhile "knowledge comes easily to the discerning." Same search, very different results.
The proverb says the mocker "seeks wisdom and finds none." Plenty is what comes easily to somebody else: "knowledge comes easily to the discerning." The mocker's search comes up empty.
Late would at least be something, friend. But the proverb gives the mocker nothing at all: he "seeks wisdom and finds none." It's the discerning who find knowledge, and they find it easily.

The proverb says the opposite. It tells you to "Stay away from a foolish man," and the reason it gives is "you will gain no knowledge from his speech." Listening longer doesn't change that. The text says none.

Yes, false. The proverb says, "Stay away from a foolish man; you will gain no knowledge from his speech." No knowledge, not a little, not eventually. Save your listening time for somebody who has something to teach.
Yes. "The folly of fools deceives them." The fool ends up fooled by his own folly. The prudent man looks at his way, and the fool's own folly leads him on.
Protection isn't what folly hands out. The proverb says "the folly of fools deceives them." If anything protects a person in these verses, it's the lips of the wise (Proverbs 14:3).
You'd hope folly would at least teach a lesson, wouldn't you? The proverb says it "deceives them." The prudent are the ones who discern their way, and the fool's own folly leads him along.

That's the one: "no stranger shares in its joy." The heart knows its own bitterness, and it also has joys that an outsider can't fully enter. I think that's why it helps to have people close enough to be more than strangers.

The proverb doesn't name a brother here. It says "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy." The word is stranger. Someone far from the heart can't share what's inside it.
No servant in this one, friend. The line is "no stranger shares in its joy." The heart's bitterness and joy are its own, and a stranger doesn't get in on them.

The proverb says it the other way around. "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish." So it's the wicked man's house that comes down. The upright man's tent is the one that flourishes.
That's right. The house of the wicked "will be destroyed," and "the tent of the upright will flourish." A big house doesn't save you if it's the wicked man's. The smaller tent does better in the end.

That's what the verse says: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." It's a heavy line, and I'll let it be heavy. A way can feel right all the way down the road, and the verse still tells you where it ends.
The proverb says it's true, friend. "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." That's a heavy one. Seeming right and being right aren't the same thing.
The proverb says otherwise. "Even in laughter the heart may ache." A laugh can be on the outside while the ache stays on the inside. And the verse adds that "joy may end in sorrow."

Right, because the verse says "Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow." Laughing and hurting can happen at the same time. So if somebody's laughing, I think it's worth being kind anyway.
That's the word. "A good man is rewarded for his ways." The backslider gets the fill of his own ways, and the good man gets rewarded for his. Each one gets what his ways bring.
A warning would be fair, but that's not what the text says. It says "a good man is rewarded for his ways." The backslider is the one who gets "the fill of his own ways."
Nobody's forgotten in this line, friend. The good man "is rewarded for his ways." That's the other side of the backslider getting the fill of his own.
Yes. "The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps." Every word, no checking. The prudent man looks where he's putting his feet.
The simple man isn't the doubter in this proverb. He's the opposite: he "believes every word." It's the prudent man who watches his steps.
Forgetting would be a different problem. The proverb says the simple man "believes every word." The prudent man is the one who "watches his steps."
That's the word. "A fool is careless and reckless." Careless and reckless, a two-for-one. The wise man, meanwhile, "fears and turns from evil."
Cautious belongs on the wise man's side. He "fears and turns from evil." The fool is "careless and reckless."
Humble is a nice word, but the proverb doesn't use it for the fool. It says a fool is "careless and reckless." The wise man is the one who turns from evil.
That's the first blank. "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly." The short fuse goes off before the thinking starts.
That's the second blank. "A devious man is hated." Sneaky doesn't win people over.
Wisely doesn't fit the short fuse. The proverb says the quick-tempered man "acts foolishly." Wisdom shows up later in the chapter, on the patient man's side (Proverbs 14:29).
Trusted is what a devious man would love to be, friend. But the text says "a devious man is hated." That's the word that fits the blank.
Honored is a big word for somebody who's devious. The proverb says "a devious man is hated." The honor in this passage goes elsewhere, like the king delighting in a wise servant (Proverbs 14:35).
The verse says it the other way around. "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous." The bowing goes toward the good. The evil are the ones doing it.
Yes, false. "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous." The good aren't the ones bowing. The evil are.

That's what the verse says: "many are those who love the rich." The proverb is describing how things go, and it's a hard one. The poor man is "hated even by his neighbor." It doesn't say that's how it should be.

The proverb doesn't say anything about a humble man here. It says "many are those who love the rich." The poor man is the one "hated even by his neighbor." It's a hard line, and it doesn't call that fair.
Honesty is praised elsewhere in this chapter, but not in this verse. Here it says "many are those who love the rich." It's a hard line, since the poor man is "hated even by his neighbor."
That's what it says: "blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor." It comes right after "He who despises his neighbor sins." Two choices, and the proverb says which one is blessed.
The proverb says the opposite of that. "Blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor." The one who "despises his neighbor sins." Kindness is the blessed side.
Yes, "those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." Planning goodness is the work, and devotion and faithfulness are what they find. The ones who contrive evil "go astray."
The proverb doesn't promise an easy road. It says "those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." The only ones with a road problem in this verse are those who "go astray."
No seat is mentioned here. The text says "those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." Devotion and faithfulness are what they find, and that's worth more than a good chair.
The proverb separates the two. "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty." Labor brings profit. Talk alone doesn't.
Right. "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty." Notice it says all labor. Talking about the work isn't doing the work, friend.
Yes. "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." The refuge isn't only for him. His children get one too.
The proverb says the opposite. "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." His children are included in that refuge.
That's it. The fear of the LORD is "a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." It gives life and it turns him away from snares. Both halves are in one verse.
Money doesn't come up in this verse. It says the fear of the LORD is "a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." Snares of death are what it turns him from.
That's not in the verse, friend. The fear of the LORD is "a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." The snares of death are what get turned away from.
Yes, "a lack of subjects is a prince's ruin." A king's splendor is a large population, and without people the prince is ruined. Splendor on one side, ruin on the other.
Joy goes with the other half. The proverb says "a large population is a king's splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince's ruin." No subjects means ruin.
Pride isn't what the text gives the prince here. It says "a lack of subjects is a prince's ruin." The splendor comes with the large population.
The proverb says the opposite. "A patient man has great understanding." Great understanding, not slow understanding. The quick-tempered man is the one who "promotes folly."
Right. "A patient man has great understanding." Waiting isn't the same as being slow. It's the quick-tempered man who "promotes folly."
That's the one: "envy rots the bones." A tranquil heart is life to the body, and envy does the reverse. It's an ugly word for an ugly thing.
Gratitude isn't in this verse. The text says "a tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones." Envy is the one that rots.
Kindness shows up in the next few verses, but not as the bone-rotter. This verse says "a tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones." Kindness is on the side of life.
That's the word. "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker." The proverb ties how a person treats the poor to the One who made them. And "whoever is kind to the needy honors Him."
The proverb says the opposite. "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker." It's the one who is kind to the needy who honors Him.
Serving is the other direction, friend. The text says "whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker." Honor goes to whoever is kind to the needy.
Yes. "The righteous man has a refuge even in death." The wicked man is thrown down by his own sin, but the righteous man still has a refuge when death comes.
The proverb doesn't limit the refuge to his house. It says "the righteous man has a refuge even in death." Even in death is a lot wider than a house.
Friends aren't mentioned in this verse. The text says "the righteous man has a refuge even in death." That refuge goes as far as death.
That's the first blank. "Righteousness exalts a nation." It lifts a nation up.
That's the second blank. "Sin is a disgrace to any people." Righteousness lifts up, and sin brings disgrace.
Divides doesn't fit the first blank. The proverb says "Righteousness exalts a nation." Exalting is the lifting up.
Blessing is the opposite of what sin brings in this verse. It says "sin is a disgrace to any people." Disgrace is the word for the second blank.
A shield would be a gift, and sin doesn't hand those out. The proverb says "sin is a disgrace to any people." Righteousness is what lifts a nation.
Yes. "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." The wise servant gets the king's delight, and the shameful get his anger. Know which servant you'd rather be.
The king's favor goes to the other servant. The proverb says "a king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." Anger is what falls on the shameful.
Silence isn't what the verse says. It says "his anger falls on the shameful." Delight goes to the wise servant, and anger goes to the shameful.
